claim: Cannabidiol (CBD) is a chemical found in the Cannabis sativa plant.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), a chemical found in the Cannabis sativa plant, is a clinically effective antiepileptic drug whose mechanism of action is unknown.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CBD's botanical origin.

claim: CBD is a clinically effective antiepileptic drug.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), a chemical found in the Cannabis sativa plant, is a clinically effective antiepileptic drug whose mechanism of action is unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical trials in the Introduction section (Devinsky et al., 2017; Devinsky et al., 2018b; Devinsky et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2020; Devinsky et al., 2018a; Thiele et al., 2019).

claim: The mechanism of action of CBD as an antiepileptic drug is unknown.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), a chemical found in the Cannabis sativa plant, is a clinically effective antiepileptic drug whose mechanism of action is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of scientific knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: CBD enhances flux through heterologously expressed human Kv7.2/7.3 channels.
source: Using a fluorescence-based thallium flux assay, we performed a large-scale screen and found enhancement of flux through heterologously expressed human Kv7.2/7.3 channels by CBD.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the thallium flux assay screen performed by the authors.

claim: CBD acts at submicromolar concentrations to shift the voltage dependence of Kv7.2/7.3 channels in the hyperpolarizing direction.
source: Patch-clamp recordings showed that CBD acts at submicromolar concentrations to shift the voltage dependence of Kv7.2/7.3 channels in the hyperpolarizing direction, producing a dramatic enhancement of current at voltages near –50 mV.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data presented in Figure 1.

claim: CBD produces a dramatic enhancement of Kv7.2/7.3 current at voltages near –50 mV.
source: Patch-clamp recordings showed that CBD acts at submicromolar concentrations to shift the voltage dependence of Kv7.2/7.3 channels in the hyperpolarizing direction, producing a dramatic enhancement of current at voltages near –50 mV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: CBD enhanced native M-current in mouse superior cervical ganglion starting at concentrations of 30 nM.
source: CBD enhanced native M-current in mouse superior cervical ganglion starting at concentrations of 30 nM and also enhanced M-current in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: CBD enhanced M-current in rat hippocampal neurons.
source: CBD enhanced native M-current in mouse superior cervical ganglion starting at concentrations of 30 nM and also enhanced M-current in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The potent enhancement of Kv7.2/7.3 channels by CBD may contribute to its effectiveness as an antiepileptic drug by reducing neuronal hyperexcitability.
source: The potent enhancement of Kv2/7.3 channels by CBD may contribute to its effectiveness as an antiepileptic drug by reducing neuronal hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: CBD is a phytocannabinoid present in marijuana.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), a phytocannabinoid present in marijuana (Mechoulam et al., 1970), has been shown in recent clinical trials to be an effective agent for treating some forms of epilepsy in children, including Dravet syndrome (Devinsky et al., 2017; Devinsky et al., 2018b; Devinsky et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2020) and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (Devinsky et al., 2018a; Thiele et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mechoulam et al., 1970.

claim: CBD has been shown in recent clinical trials to be an effective agent for treating Dravet syndrome.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), a phytocannabinoid present in marijuana (Mechoulam et al., 1970), has been shown in recent clinical trials to be an effective agent for treating some forms of epilepsy in children, including Dravet syndrome (Devinsky et al., 2017; Devinsky et al., 2018b; Devinsky et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2020) and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (Devinsky et al., 2018a; Thiele et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical trials (Devinsky et al., 2017; Devinsky et al., 2018b; Devinsky et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2020).

claim: CBD has been shown in recent clinical trials to be an effective agent for treating Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
source: Cannabidiol (CBD), a phytocannabinoid present in marijuana (Mechoulam et al., 1970), has been shown in recent clinical trials to be an effective agent for treating some forms of epilepsy in children, including Dravet syndrome (Devinsky et al., 2017; Devinsky et al., 2018b; Devinsky et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2020) and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (Devinsky et al., 2018a; Thiele et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trials (Devinsky et al., 2018a; Thiele et al., 2019).

claim: How CBD ameliorates epileptic activity is unclear.
source: How CBD ameliorates epileptic activity is unclear (Rosenberg et al., 2015; Rosenberg et al., 2017; Franco and Perucca, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Unlike Δ(9)-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), CBD does not activate CB1 or CB2 G-protein-coupled receptors.
source: Unlike Δ(9)-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the other major phytocannabinoid in marijuana, CBD does not activate CB1 or CB2 G-protein-coupled receptors (Pertwee, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pertwee, 2005.

claim: At micromolar concentrations, CBD has inhibitory effects on a wide range of proteins, including many receptors and channels.
source: At micromolar concentrations, CBD has inhibitory effects on a wide range of proteins, including many receptors and channels (Ibeas Bih et al., 2015; Watkins, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ibeas Bih et al., 2015 and Watkins, 2019.

claim: CBD inhibits voltage-dependent sodium channels in a state-dependent manner, with reported half-maximal concentrations of ~2–10 μM.
source: Like many classic antiepileptic agents, CBD inhibits voltage-dependent sodium channels in a state-dependent manner, with reported half-maximal concentrations of ~2–10 μM (Hill et al., 2014; Patel et al., 2016; Ghovanloo et al., 2018; Mason and Cummins, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: CBD reduction of overall epileptiform activity can be detected in brain slice preparations at much lower concentrations than those required for sodium channel inhibition.
source: However, as CBD reduction of overall epileptiform activity can be detected in brain slice preparations at much lower concentrations (Jones et al., 2010), the importance of sodium channel inhibition for CBD's anticonvulsant effects remains uncertain (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jones et al., 2010.

claim: The importance of sodium channel inhibition for CBD's anticonvulsant effects remains uncertain.
source: However, as CBD reduction of overall epileptiform activity can be detected in brain slice preparations at much lower concentrations (Jones et al., 2010), the importance of sodium channel inhibition for CBD's anticonvulsant effects remains uncertain (Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between concentrations needed for sodium channel inhibition and those showing anticonvulsant effects, supported by citations.

claim: CBD acts as an antagonist of the lipid-activated G-protein-coupled receptor GPR55.
source: Other molecular targets that could mediate antiepileptic actions of CBD have been described, notably antagonism of the lipid-activated G-protein-coupled receptor GPR55 (Ryberg et al., 2007; Sylantyev et al., 2013; Kaplan et al., 2017), and electrophysiological effects correlated with GPR55 antagonism have been described at concentrations of CBD as low as 200 nM (Sylantyev et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ryberg et al., 2007; Sylantyev et al., 2013; Kaplan et al., 2017.

claim: Electrophysiological effects correlated with GPR55 antagonism have been described at concentrations of CBD as low as 200 nM.
source: Other molecular targets that could mediate antiepileptic actions of CBD have been described, notably antagonism of the lipid-activated G-protein-coupled receptor GPR55 (Ryberg et al., 2007; Sylantyev et al., 2013; Kaplan et al., 2017), and electrophysiological effects correlated with GPR55 antagonism have been described at concentrations of CBD as low as 200 nM (Sylantyev et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sylantyev et al., 2013.

claim: The most potent effect of CBD on a well-defined electrophysiological function so far reported is an inhibition of endocannabinoid modulation of synaptic transmission.
source: The most potent effect of CBD on a well-defined electrophysiological function so far reported is an inhibition of endocannabinoid modulation of synaptic transmission (Straiker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Straiker et al., 2018.

claim: CBD's inhibition of endocannabinoid modulation of synaptic transmission is mediated by a negative allosteric effect on CB1 receptors.
source: This effect of CBD is mediated by a negative allosteric effect on CB1 receptors, with CBD acting at a site distinct from the primary binding site (Laprairie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Laprairie et al., 2015.

claim: CBD acts at a site distinct from the primary binding site on CB1 receptors.
source: This effect of CBD is mediated by a negative allosteric effect on CB1 receptors, with CBD acting at a site distinct from the primary binding site (Laprairie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Laprairie et al., 2015.

claim: CBD's inhibitory negative allosteric effect on CB1 receptors is detectable at 100 nM and is substantial at 500 nM.
source: Electrophysiologically, this inhibitory negative allosteric effect is detectable at 100 nM and is substantial at 500 nM (Straiker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Straiker et al., 2018.

claim: CBD acts at concentrations as low as 30 nM to activate neuronal M-current.
source: Here, we report that CBD acts at concentrations as low as 30 nM to activate neuronal M-current, a non-inactivating potassium current mediated by Kv7 channels that activate at subthreshold voltages.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: M-current is a non-inactivating potassium current mediated by Kv7 channels that activate at subthreshold voltages.
source: Here, we report that CBD acts at concentrations as low as 30 nM to activate neuronal M-current, a non-inactivating potassium current mediated by Kv7 channels that activate at subthreshold voltages.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about M-current.

claim: CBD shifts the voltage dependence of activation of Kv7 channels in the hyperpolarizing direction.
source: CBD shifts the voltage dependence of activation of these channels in the hyperpolarizing direction, resulting in a significant activation of Kv7 current at subthreshold voltages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: CBD's shift in voltage dependence results in a significant activation of Kv7 current at subthreshold voltages.
source: CBD shifts the voltage dependence of activation of these channels in the hyperpolarizing direction, resulting in a significant activation of Kv7 current at subthreshold voltages.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing the voltage shift and current enhancement.

claim: The activation of neuronal M-current may be one mechanism by which CBD exerts its antiepileptic action.
source: These results suggest that the activation of neuronal M-current may be one mechanism by which CBD exerts its antiepileptic action.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: In a screen of 154 compounds, CBD was the only compound to produce a substantial enhancement of the fluorescence signal, except for retigabine and flupirtine.
source: In a screen of a library of 154 compounds chosen from structures with known or possible ion channel modulating activity (Figure 1—source data 1), CBD was the only compound to produce a substantial enhancement of the fluorescence signal, except for retigabine and flupirtine, both known activators of Kv7.2/7.3 channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the thallium flux assay screen.

claim: Retigabine and flupirtine are known activators of Kv7.2/7.3 channels.
source: In a screen of a library of 154 compounds chosen from structures with known or possible ion channel modulating activity (Figure 1—source data 1), CBD was the only compound to produce a substantial enhancement of the fluorescence signal, except for retigabine and flupirtine, both known activators of Kv7.2/7.3 channels.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about these compounds.

claim: 100 nM CBD produced a doubling of the current activated at –50 mV in Kv7.2/7.3 channels.
source: Figure 1A shows an example, where 100 nM CBD produced a doubling of the current activated at –50 mV, while there was little effect at –20 mV, where channels are near-maximally activated in the control situation.
evidence: This is supported by the example shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 100 nM CBD had little effect on Kv7.2/7.3 current at –20 mV, where channels are near-maximally activated in the control situation.
source: Figure 1A shows an example, where 100 nM CBD produced a doubling of the current activated at –50 mV, while there was little effect at –20 mV, where channels are near-maximally activated in the control situation.
evidence: This is supported by the example shown in Figure 1A and reflects the mechanism of action (voltage shift).

claim: 100 nM CBD enhanced the current evoked at –50 mV by an average factor of 2.8 ± 0.4 (n = 20).
source: 100 nM enhanced the current evoked at –50 mV by an average factor of 2.8 ± 0.4 (n = 20), while 300 nM CBD enhanced the current by a factor of 4.6 ± 0.5 (n = 14).
evidence: This is quantitative data from patch-clamp experiments, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 300 nM CBD enhanced the current evoked at –50 mV by a factor of 4.6 ± 0.5 (n = 14).
source: 100 nM enhanced the current evoked at –50 mV by an average factor of 2.8 ± 0.4 (n = 20), while 300 nM CBD enhanced the current by a factor of 4.6 ± 0.5 (n = 14).
evidence: This is quantitative data from patch-clamp experiments, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 300 nM CBD shifted the midpoint for channel activation by an average of –13.9 ± 0.9 mV (n = 17).
source: In collected results, 300 nM CBD shifted the midpoint for channel activation by an average of –13.9 ± 0.9 mV (n = 17).
evidence: This is quantitative data from voltage-dependence experiments.

claim: The shift in the voltage dependence of activation reached a maximum of about –20 mV at CBD concentrations of 3–10 μM.
source: The shift in the voltage dependence of activation reached a maximum of about –20 mV at CBD concentrations of 3–10 μM, with CBD acting with a half-maximal concentration of about 200 nM (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the concentration-response data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CBD acts with a half-maximal concentration of about 200 nM to shift the voltage dependence of Kv7.2/7.3 activation.
source: The shift in the voltage dependence of activation reached a maximum of about –20 mV at CBD concentrations of 3–10 μM, with CBD acting with a half-maximal concentration of about 200 nM (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the concentration-response curve and Hill equation fit shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CBD shifted the voltage dependence of M-current in SCG neurons, resulting in less complete deactivation for a step to –60 mV.
source: It was also clear that CBD shifted the voltage dependence of M-current, resulting in less complete deactivation for a step to –60 mV (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental traces shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The enhancement of M-current measured at –50 mV increased from a factor of 1.85 ± 0.19 with 30 nM CBD (n = 14) to a factor of 3.02 ± 0.56 with 300 nM CBD (n = 9).
source: In collected results quantifying the effect of CBD, the enhancement of M-current measured at –50 mV increased from a factor of 1.85 ± 0.19 with 30 nm CBD (n = 14) to a factor of 3.02 ± 0.56 with 300 nm CBD (n = 9).
evidence: This is quantitative data from SCG neuron experiments, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CBD enhancement of M-current in hippocampal neurons occurs in 16 of the 20 cells tested.
source: Using a voltage protocol designed to emphasize M-current (holding the neurons at –30 mV and stepping to –50 mV), CBD enhanced the outward current at both –30 mV and –50 mV in 16 of the 20 cells tested.
evidence: This is quantitative data from hippocampal neuron experiments.

claim: There was no increase in current if CBD was applied in the presence of the Kv7 inhibitor XE-991.
source: Consistent with this action of CBD being an enhancement of M-current, which in hippocampal neurons is mediated by Kv7.2, Kv7.3, and Kv7.5 (Shah et al., 2002), there was no increase if CBD was applied in the presence of the Kv7 inhibitor XE-991 (Wang et al., 1998; Brown and Passmore, 2009).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3, demonstrating specificity of CBD's effect on Kv7 channels.

claim: M-current in hippocampal neurons is mediated by Kv7.2, Kv7.3, and Kv7.5.
source: Consistent with this action of CBD being an enhancement of M-current, which in hippocampal neurons is mediated by Kv7.2, Kv7.3, and Kv7.5 (Shah et al., 2002), there was no increase if CBD was applied in the presence of the Kv7 inhibitor XE-991 (Wang et al., 1998; Brown and Passmore, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shah et al., 2002.

claim: CBD applied after XE-991 produced on average a small (13% ± 4%, n = 15) decrease in current at –50 mV.
source: In fact, CBD applied after XE-991 produced on average a small (13% ± 4%, n = 15) decrease in current at –50 mV, consistent with a weak inhibitory effect on other, non-M-currents.
evidence: This is quantitative data from hippocampal neuron experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: CBD has a weak inhibitory effect on other, non-M-currents in hippocampal neurons.
source: In fact, CBD applied after XE-991 produced on average a small (13% ± 4%, n = 15) decrease in current at –50 mV, consistent with a weak inhibitory effect on other, non-M-currents.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that CBD decreases current when M-current is blocked.

claim: Kv7 channel-mediated M-current plays a major role in controlling the excitability of many types of neurons, including neocortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Kv7 channel-mediated M-current plays a major role in controlling the excitability of many types of neurons, including neocortical pyramidal neurons (Barrese et al., 2018; Brown and Passmore, 2009; Gunthorpe et al., 2012; Vigil et al., 2020; Jepps et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Enhancement of M-current is a clinically proven mechanism of antiepileptic action.
source: Enhancement of M-current is a clinically proven mechanism of antiepileptic action, as demonstrated by the clinical efficacy of retigabine, an antiepileptic drug that acts by enhancement of current through Kv7 channels (Wickenden et al., 2000; Tatulian et al., 2001; Gunthorpe et al., 2012; Sills and Rogawski, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on retigabine.

claim: Retigabine is an antiepileptic drug that acts by enhancement of current through Kv7 channels.
source: Enhancement of M-current is a clinically proven mechanism of antiepileptic action, as demonstrated by the clinical efficacy of retigabine, an antiepileptic drug that acts by enhancement of current through Kv7 channels (Wickenden et al., 2000; Tatulian et al., 2001; Gunthorpe et al., 2012; Sills and Rogawski, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The clinical efficacy of CBD could result at least in part by the enhancement of the Kv7-mediated M-current in central neurons.
source: Our results suggest that the clinical efficacy of CBD could result at least in part by the enhancement of the Kv7-mediated M-current in central neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The effect of CBD in enhancing the neuronal M-current is the opposite of the effect of cannabinoids that act as agonists at the CB1 receptor, which inhibit M-current in hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, the effect of CBD in enhancing the neuronal M-current is the opposite of the effect of cannabinoids that act as agonists at the CB1 receptor, which inhibit M-current in hippocampal neurons (Schweitzer, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schweitzer, 2000.

claim: Cannabinoids that act as agonists at the CB1 receptor inhibit M-current in hippocampal neurons.
source: Interestingly, the effect of CBD in enhancing the neuronal M-current is the opposite of the effect of cannabinoids that act as agonists at the CB1 receptor, which inhibit M-current in hippocampal neurons (Schweitzer, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schweitzer, 2000.

claim: The fact that CBD is not a CB1 agonist and actually acts as an allosteric antagonist at CB1 receptors may be an important aspect of its mechanism of action.
source: Thus, the fact that CBD is not a CB1 agonist – and actually acts as an allosteric antagonist at CB1 receptors (Laprairie et al., 2015; Straiker et al., 2018) – may be an important aspect of its mechanism of action.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The opposite effects on M-current of CBD and CB1 agonists like THC fit well with the history of the development of CBD as an antiepileptic drug.
source: The opposite effects on M-current of CBD and CB1 agonists like THC fit well with the history of the development of CBD as an antiepileptic drug, which began with anecdotal evidence that extracts from a particular strain of cannabis with high CBD and low THC ('Charlotte's Web') were an effective adjunctive therapy for a child with Dravet syndrome (Maa and Figi, 2014; Rosenberg et al., 2015; Williams and Stephens, 2020).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the experimental findings to the historical development of CBD therapy, supported by citations.

claim: The development of CBD as an antiepileptic drug began with anecdotal evidence that extracts from a particular strain of cannabis with high CBD and low THC ('Charlotte's Web') were an effective adjunctive therapy for a child with Dravet syndrome.
source: The opposite effects on M-current of CBD and CB1 agonists like THC fit well with the history of the development of CBD as an antiepileptic drug, which began with anecdotal evidence that extracts from a particular strain of cannabis with high CBD and low THC ('Charlotte's Web') were an effective adjunctive therapy for a child with Dravet syndrome (Maa and Figi, 2014; Rosenberg et al., 2015; Williams and Stephens, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Maa and Figi, 2014; Rosenberg et al., 2015; Williams and Stephens, 2020.

claim: Use of plastic containers and plastic tubing could greatly reduce the apparent effects of solutions with CBD at submicromolar concentrations.
source: In doing our experiments, an important step was discovering that use of plastic containers and plastic tubing could greatly reduce the apparent effects of solutions with CBD at submicromolar concentrations, likely reflecting loss of CBD by absorption into plastic as occurs with other cannabinoids with similarly high lipophilicity (Christophersen, 1986; Hippalgaonkar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experimental work, supported by citations about cannabinoid absorption into plastic.

claim: Loss of CBD by absorption into plastic occurs as with other cannabinoids with similarly high lipophilicity.
source: In doing our experiments, an important step was discovering that use of plastic containers and plastic tubing could greatly reduce the apparent effects of solutions with CBD at submicromolar concentrations, likely reflecting loss of CBD by absorption into plastic as occurs with other cannabinoids with similarly high lipophilicity (Christophersen, 1986; Hippalgaonkar et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Christophersen, 1986 and Hippalgaonkar et al., 2011.

claim: When using glass reservoirs and tubing to apply well-defined concentrations of CBD to isolated neurons, substantial inhibition of steady-state 'persistent' sodium current can be seen with 30–100 nM CBD.
source: Although published data for CBD inhibition of sodium channels have typically reported half-blocking concentrations of 2–10 μM, we have found that when using glass reservoirs and tubing to apply well-defined concentrations of CBD to isolated neurons, substantial inhibition of steady-state 'persistent' sodium current can be seen with 30–100 nM CBD (unpublished results).
evidence: This is based on unpublished experimental data from the authors.

claim: CBD at 100 nM significantly depresses endocannabinoid modulation of synaptic transmission.
source: CBD at 100 nM also significantly depresses endocannabinoid modulation of synaptic transmission (Straiker et al., 2018), suggesting that the overall effects of submicromolar concentrations of CBD on neuronal excitability could involve multiple actions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Straiker et al., 2018.

claim: The overall effects of submicromolar concentrations of CBD on neuronal excitability could involve multiple actions.
source: CBD at 100 nM also significantly depresses endocannabinoid modulation of synaptic transmission (Straiker et al., 2018), suggesting that the overall effects of submicromolar concentrations of CBD on neuronal excitability could involve multiple actions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the multiple effects of CBD at similar concentrations.

claim: Kv7.2/7.3 channels are susceptible to enhancement by a wide variety of agents acting by several different mechanisms.
source: Our results add to recent experiments demonstrating that Kv7.2/7.3 channels are susceptible to enhancement by a wide variety of agents acting by several different mechanisms (De Silva et al., 2018; Manville and Abbott, 2018c; Manville and Abbott, 2018a; Miceli et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; Kanyo et al., 2020; Kurata, 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: Agents that enhance Kv7.2/7.3 channels include endogenous compounds like GABA.
source: Such agents include endogenous compounds like GABA (Manville et al., 2018b), the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (Manville et al., 2020), and arachidonic acid metabolites and derivatives (Schweitzer et al., 1990; Schweitzer et al., 1993; Larsson et al., 2020a; Larsson et al., 2020b), as well as a variety of natural products including cilantro (Manville and Abbott, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Manville et al., 2018b.

claim: Agents that enhance Kv7.2/7.3 channels include the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate.
source: Such agents include endogenous compounds like GABA (Manville et al., 2018b), the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (Manville et al., 2020), and arachidonic acid metabolites and derivatives (Schweitzer et al., 1990; Schweitzer et al., 1993; Larsson et al., 2020a; Larsson et al., 2020b), as well as a variety of natural products including cilantro (Manville and Abbott, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Manville et al., 2020.

claim: Agents that enhance Kv7.2/7.3 channels include arachidonic acid metabolites and derivatives.
source: Such agents include endogenous compounds like GABA (Manville et al., 2018b), the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (Manville et al., 2020), and arachidonic acid metabolites and derivatives (Schweitzer et al., 1990; Schweitzer et al., 1993; Larsson et al., 2020a; Larsson et al., 2020b), as well as a variety of natural products including cilantro (Manville and Abbott, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schweitzer et al., 1990; Schweitzer et al., 1993; Larsson et al., 2020a; Larsson et al., 2020b.

claim: Agents that enhance Kv7.2/7.3 channels include natural products like cilantro.
source: Such agents include endogenous compounds like GABA (Manville et al., 2018b), the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate (Manville et al., 2020), and arachidonic acid metabolites and derivatives (Schweitzer et al., 1990; Schweitzer et al., 1993; Larsson et al., 2020a; Larsson et al., 2020b), as well as a variety of natural products including cilantro (Manville and Abbott, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Manville and Abbott, 2019.

claim: Further development of Kv7.2/7.3 enhancers for treating epilepsy and other neuronal disorders seems promising.
source: Further development of Kv7.2/7.3 enhancers for treating epilepsy and other neuronal disorders seems promising (Maljevic and Lerche, 2014; Vigil et al., 2020), especially because retigabine has been withdrawn from clinical use because of a number of off-target side effects (Brickel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Retigabine has been withdrawn from clinical use because of a number of off-target side effects.
source: Further development of Kv7.2/7.3 enhancers for treating epilepsy and other neuronal disorders seems promising (Maljevic and Lerche, 2014; Vigil et al., 2020), especially because retigabine has been withdrawn from clinical use because of a number of off-target side effects (Brickel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brickel et al., 2020.

claim: Compared to other compounds recently found to enhance Kv7.2/7.3 channels, CBD has the distinction of having already been successfully used in multiple epilepsy clinical trials.
source: Compared to other compounds recently found to enhance Kv7.2/7.3 channels, CBD has the distinction of having already been successfully used in multiple epilepsy clinical trials.
evidence: This is based on the clinical trial data cited earlier in the manuscript.

claim: CBD is far from a perfect drug as it requires large dosages and has a complex pharmacokinetic profile that limit its effective oral administration.
source: However, CBD is far from a perfect drug (Sekar and Pack, 2019) as it requires large dosages and has a complex pharmacokinetic profile that limit its effective oral administration (Millar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sekar and Pack, 2019 and Millar et al., 2019.

claim: Improved knowledge of CBD's most important molecular targets should allow for the design of novel compounds that retain its key molecular actions but with improved pharmacokinetics and reduced off-target effects.
source: Improved knowledge of CBD's most important molecular targets should allow for the design of novel compounds that retain its key molecular actions but with improved pharmacokinetics and reduced off-target effects.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future drug development.

claim: In the voltage-dependent activation experiment, 300 nM CBD shifted the control Vhn from –54.4 mV to –67.9 mV.
source: Control: Vhn = –54.4 mV, k = 12.8 mV (midpoint of function = –33.1); 300 nM CBD: Vhn = –67.9 mV, k = 11.8 mV (midpoint of function –48.3 mV).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Boltzmann fits shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The EC50 for CBD's shift of activation midpoint is 214 nM with a Hill coefficient of 1.3.
source: Solid line: fit to the Hill equation, ΔVh = −2.5 mV − 17.5 mV/(1 + (EC50/[CBD])^nH), where EC50 = 214 nM and the Hill coefficient nH = 1.3.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the Hill equation fit shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 30 nM CBD significantly enhanced M-current at –50 mV compared to no CBD control (p=0.024).
source: Non-paired two-tailed t-tests: 10 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.85; 30 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.024; 100 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.015; 300 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.012.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 100 nM CBD significantly enhanced M-current at –50 mV compared to no CBD control (p=0.015).
source: Non-paired two-tailed t-tests: 10 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.85; 30 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.024; 100 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.015; 300 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.012.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 300 nM CBD significantly enhanced M-current at –50 mV compared to no CBD control (p=0.012).
source: Non-paired two-tailed t-tests: 10 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.85; 30 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.024; 100 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.015; 300 nM CBD vs. No CBD, p=0.012.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 2B.
